{{Short description|Probability distribution of random variable}}
In [[probability theory]], '''Chernoff's distribution''', named after [[Herman Chernoff]], is the [[probability distribution]] of the [[random variable]]

: <math> Z =\underset{s \in \mathbf{R}}{\operatorname{argmax}}\ (W(s) - s^2), </math>

where ''W'' is a "two-sided" [[Wiener process]] (or two-sided "[[Brownian motion]]") satisfying ''W''(0)&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.  
If

: <math> V(a,c) = \underset{s \in \mathbf{R}}{\operatorname{argmax}} \ (W(s) - c(s-a)^2), </math>

then ''V''(0,&nbsp;''c'') has density

: <math> f_c(t) = \frac{1}{2} g_c(t) g_c(-t) </math>

where ''g''<sub>''c''</sub> has [[Fourier transform]] given by

: <math> \hat{g}_c (s) = \frac{(2/c)^{1/3}}{\operatorname{Ai} (i (2c^2)^{-1/3} s)}, \ \ \ s \in \mathbf{R} </math>

and where Ai is the [[Airy function]].  Thus ''f''<sub>''c''</sub> is symmetric about 0 and the density&nbsp;''&fnof;''<sub>''Z''</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''&fnof;''<sub>1</sub>. Groeneboom (1989)<ref>{{cite journal
|first= Piet |last = Groeneboom|title =Brownian motion with a parabolic drift and Airy functions
|journal= Probability Theory and Related Fields|volume = 81|pages=79&ndash;109
|year=1989| doi=10.1007/BF00343738|mr=981568
| s2cid=119980629 |url = https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/6435|doi-access=free}}</ref> shows that

:<math> f_Z (z) \sim \frac{1}{2} \frac{4^{4/3} |z|}{\operatorname{Ai}' (\tilde{a}_1)} \exp \left( - \frac{2}{3} |z|^3 + 2^{1/3} \tilde{a}_1 |z| \right)
\text{ as }z \rightarrow \infty
</math>

where <math>\tilde{a}_1 \approx -2.3381</math> is the largest zero of the Airy function Ai and where <math>\operatorname{Ai}' (\tilde{a}_1 ) \approx 0.7022</math>. In the same paper, Groeneboom also gives an analysis of the [[stochastic process|process]] <math>\{V(a,1): a \in \mathbf{R}\}</math>. The connection with the statistical problem of estimating a monotone density is discussed in Groeneboom (1985).<ref>{{cite book|last=Groeneboom|first=Piet|year=1985|
title=Estimating a monotone density|editor1=Le Cam, L.E.|editor2=Olshen, R. A.|series=Proceedings of the Berkeley conference in honor of Jerzy Neyman and Jack Kiefer, vol. II| pages=539&ndash;555}}
</ref> Chernoff's distribution is now known to appear in a wide range of monotone problems including [[isotonic regression]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Some Developments in the Theory of Shape Constrained Inference|last1=Groeneboom|first1=Piet|last2=Jongbloed|first2=Geurt|journal=[[Statistical Science]]|volume=33|issue=4|year=2018|pages=473–492|doi=10.1214/18-STS657 |s2cid=13672538 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

The Chernoff distribution should not be confused with the Chernoff geometric distribution<ref>{{cite journal | first= Frank |
last= Nielsen|
title=Revisiting Chernoff Information with Likelihood Ratio Exponential Families
| journal = Entropy
| publisher= MDPI
 | year=2022 | 
doi=10.3390/e24101400  | 
volume=24 | 
number =10|
page= 1400|
pmid= 37420420|
pmc= 9601539|
doi-access= free}}</ref>  (called the Chernoff point in information geometry) induced by the Chernoff information.

== History == 
Groeneboom, Lalley and Temme<ref name="GLT16">{{cite journal|title=Chernoff's distribution and differential equations of parabolic and Airy type|last1=Groeneboom|first1=Piet|last2=Lalley|first2=Steven|last3=Temme|first3=Nico|journal=[[Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications]]|volume=423|issue=2|pages=1804–1824|year=2015|doi=10.1016/j.jmaa.2014.10.051 |mr=3278229|s2cid=119173815 |doi-access=free|arxiv=1305.6053}}</ref> state that the first investigation of this distribution was probably by Chernoff in 1964,<ref>{{cite journal
|first=Herman | last= Chernoff |title = Estimation of the mode| journal = Annals of the Institute of Statistical Mathematics | volume = 16 | pages=31&ndash;41|year=1964 | doi= 10.1007/BF02868560 | mr= 0172382| s2cid= 121030566 }}</ref> who studied the behavior of a certain [[estimator]] of a [[mode (statistics)|mode]]. In his paper, Chernoff characterized the distribution through an analytic representation through the [[heat equation]] with suitable [[boundary conditions]]. Initial attempts at approximating Chernoff's distribution via solving the heat equation, however, did not achieve satisfactory precision due to the nature of the boundary conditions.<ref name="GLT16"/> The computation of the distribution is addressed, for example, in Groeneboom and Wellner (2001).<ref>{{cite journal
|author1=Groeneboom, Piet  |author2=Wellner, Jon A.
|  title= Computing Chernoff's Distribution
|  journal= Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics
|  volume=10
|issue=2
|  pages=388&ndash;400
|  year=2001
|  doi=  10.1198/10618600152627997
|  mr=1939706
|citeseerx=10.1.1.369.863
|s2cid=6573960
}}</ref>

The connection of Chernoff's distribution with Airy functions was also found independently by Daniels and Skyrme<ref>{{cite journal
|first1=H.E. |last1= Daniels |first2= T.H.R. |last2= Skyrme
|title= The maximum of a random walk whose mean path has a maximum
|journal= Advances in Applied Probability |volume = 17 
|year = 1985 |issue= 1 | pages = 85&ndash;99 |doi= 10.2307/1427054 |jstor= 1427054 |mr= 0778595  |s2cid= 124603511 }}</ref> and Temme,<ref>{{cite journal
|first= N.M. |last = Temme|title =A convolution integral equation solved by Laplace transformations
|journal= Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics |volume = 12&ndash;13|pages=609&ndash;613
|year=1985| doi=10.1016/0377-0427(85)90052-4
|url = https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/2540/2540D.pdf|mr=0793989| s2cid=120496241 }}</ref> as cited in Groeneboom, Lalley and Temme. These two papers, along with Groeneboom (1989), were all written in 1984.<ref name="GLT16"/>
